extracted.intended_audience: orators, poets, literary critics, and students of rhetoric
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for producing 'the sublime' in literature and oratory: what makes style elevated, lasting, and powerful (Longinus' On the Sublime). Useful to writers, speakers, and critics seeking to create or judge sublime passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring effect / universality
rubrics_metrics.description: To be truly beautiful and sublime which pleases all people at all times; the memory of it is stubborn and indelible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True sublimity does not merely excite in the moment but 'outlasts the moment of utterance' and 'gives abundant food for thought.' If a passage, after careful consideration, sinks in esteem or fails to leave more than the mere words, it cannot be the true sublime. Unanimous agreement among diverse judges strengthens faith in a passage’s sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source 1: Command of full-blooded ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The command of full-blooded ideas (weighty and solid thought) is the first and most powerful source of the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great style is the natural outcome of weighty thoughts; sublime sayings naturally fall to men of spirit. This is largely congenital but can be trained by impregnating the mind with lofty inspiration. See Longinus' reference to 'weighty and solid thought' as central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source 2: Inspiration of vehement emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Vehement emotion (genuine emotion in the right place) is a principal source of sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotion is not identical with sublimity—some emotions are mean and not sublime, and many sublime passages lack emotion—but 'nothing makes the style so great as genuine emotion in the right place.' Emotion can 'inspire the words with the breath of madness' and fill them with divine afflatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source 3: Proper construction of figures (thought and speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper construction of figures—figures of thought and figures of speech—is a source of the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures include arrangement of words and clauses into a total effect of grandeur. Proper figures help create coherence and elevated effect; misarranged or clumsy figures spoil sublimity. Avoid gaps and irrelevant ornament that break the unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source 4: Nobility of phrase (choice of words, metaphor, ornament)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nobility of phrase, resolved into choice of words and use of metaphor and poetic ornament, is a source of grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elevated diction, apt metaphors, and tasteful ornament enrich style. Choice of striking, noble words contributes materially; metaphor and poetic ornament must be used to enhance dignity, not to dazzle or distract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source 5: General effect of dignity and elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: The general effect of dignity and elevation (the total, majestic effect) embraces the other sources and produces grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This overarching elevation is the integrating quality that makes a passage sublime: a coherent whole of lofty thought, fitting emotion, noble phrasing, and apt figures producing a dignified impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity / noble character of the speaker/author
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind behind the style must be neither small nor ignoble; the source of sublimity must be suggested and shown to be genuine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is necessary to 'suggest its source'—the noble mind—so the audience perceives the speaker as capable of sublime thought. Petty or servile thinkers cannot produce truly sublime utterances; the author's character (genius, spirit) is an implicit criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and organic combination of constituent elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublimity arises from a consistently happy choice of constituent elements and the power of combining them into an organic whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attraction lies partly in selection of ideas and partly in 'soldering' them together. The writer should choose the most striking elements and combine them so they cohere into a single elevated structure rather than a disconnected list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and compression of imagery to fit content (linguistic shaping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language should be compressed and forced into conformity with the content so as to 'figure' the experience (e.g., compressing diction to mirror disaster).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longinus praises passages that 'tortured his language into conformity with the impending disaster' and 'stamped on the diction the form and feature of the danger.' Use abnormal unions or compressed syntax to embody and intensify the subject-matter (as Homer does), rather than calm elegance that diminishes awe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of empty bombast, pedantry, and irrelevancies
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublimity must not be empty bombast; avoid affected, undignified, pedantic, or irrelevant material that spoils the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrelevancies are compared to gaps or open tracery in architecture — they 'utterly spoil the effect of sublime ideas.' Keep dignity; exclude anything that demeans or distracts from the sustained grandeur. Pedantic definition or elegant understatement can destroy awe when the situation requires overwhelming force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplification used with sublimity (amount vs elevation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amplification (accumulating aspects, development, exaggeration, laying stress, husbandry of facts/feelings) strengthens argument but differs from sublimity: amplification is amount, sublimity is elevation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amplification can take many forms (developing a commonplace, exaggeration, stressing events) and may enhance conviction, but without sublimity it becomes hollow and nerveless. Sublimity can occur in a single idea; amplification always involves quantity and accumulation. Use amplification to build force, but ensure elevation is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of the most striking, concrete symptoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose and combine the most striking, intense symptoms or images (concrete particulars) to evoke the passion or situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Sappho summons soul, body, hearing, tongue, sight, colour together — she selects the most striking signs and aggregates them to create the effect. Picking vivid, representative details and fusing them provides a sustained impression of intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamic depiction rather than bald definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict ongoing peril or emotion dynamically rather than defining it once; make the language present and repeatedly on the brink.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longinus contrasts Homer’s continuous, repeated sense of imminent danger ('again and again, with every wave on the very brink of death') with a poet who reduces danger to a single defined fact. For awe, avoid static definition; render the experience as persistent, developing, and tense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorum / fitness to subject (avoid irreligious or unfitting imagery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagery and representation must be fitting and not violate what is appropriate to the subject (e.g., irreligious or unseemly portrayals lessen sublimity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longinus criticizes passages that are 'utterly irreligious and show no sense of what is fitting.' Even powerful images must observe propriety relative to their theme; otherwise the effect is displeasing rather than sublime.
